meta.title: Who really said "Pride comes before a fall"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: "Pride comes before a fall" isn't a Bible verse. It's a truncated paraphrase of Proverbs 16:18, which actually reads: "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Pride comes before a fall'?
meta.ogDescription: Not scripture, but almost. The line is a shortened, modernised paraphrase of Proverbs 16:18 in the King James Bible.

answer.label: A paraphrase of the Bible — Proverbs 16:18
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely biblical, but the exact words are not scripture. The closest verse, Proverbs 16:18, reads in the 1611 King James Version: “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.” The familiar one-liner compresses those two clauses into one and modernises ‘goeth’ first to ‘goes’ and then to ‘comes’ — so no Bible printed the sentence as it is usually quoted.

source.heading: The verse behind the saying

docMeta.dd: “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.”
A truncated, modernised folk paraphrase — not a verse in any Bible

source.excerpt: Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
trail: Wiktionary derives the saying directly from scripture, calling it “probably a truncation of Proverbs 16:18” and printing the 1611 wording “Pride goeth before destruction: and an hautie spirit before a fall” (Wiktionary).

The King James wording of Proverbs 16:18 is “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall” — the modern ESV renders it “Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall,” and the NIV “Pride goes before destruction, a haughty spirit before a fall.”
Grammarist traces the drift in wording: the biblical “goeth” form “morphed into pride goes before a fall, and then finally, pride comes before a fall” (Grammarist).
source.excerptNote: The full KJV verse (Proverbs 16:18) is a two-part parallelism. “Pride comes before a fall” keeps ‘pride’ from the first clause and ‘a fall’ from the second, dropping ‘destruction’ and the ‘haughty spirit’ entirely.

source.rightsNote: The source text, Proverbs 16:18 in the King James Version, was first published in 1611 and is long in the public domain in the United States. The shortened proverb “pride comes before a fall” is an anonymous folk paraphrase with no identifiable modern author, so it carries no live copyright.

author.name: The Book of Proverbs
author.heading: Where the idea comes from
author.metaLine: Book of the Hebrew Bible · wisdom literature traditionally ascribed to King Solomon
author.bio: The Book of Proverbs is a collection of Hebrew wisdom sayings in the Old Testament, traditionally attributed to King Solomon though compiled over centuries. Proverbs 16:18 — “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall” in the 1611 King James Version — is the verse the popular one-liner is drawn from. The book’s terse, parallel couplets lend themselves to exactly this kind of shortening in everyday speech.

misattribution.heading: Almost scripture, but not quite
misattribution.intro: People quote “pride comes before a fall” as if it were a verse. The idea is biblical, but no Bible prints that sentence — it is a compressed, modernised paraphrase.

items.why: No translation reads “pride comes before a fall.” The King James Version of Proverbs 16:18 reads “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall” — two clauses the saying collapses into one.
Even the popular form is unstable: Grammarist notes it drifted from ‘goeth’ to ‘goes’ to ‘comes’ over time (Grammarist), so the ‘comes’ version is the furthest from any printed verse.

misattribution.truthLine: The genuine text is Proverbs 16:18 — “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall” — which Wiktionary identifies as the source the modern proverb truncates.

context.heading: Why the short form stuck
lead: Proverbs is built from tight, two-part couplets, and everyday speech tends to keep the vivid halves and drop the rest. Here the memorable pairing is ‘pride’ and ‘a fall’ — so the middle terms, ‘destruction’ and the ‘haughty spirit,’ fell away, leaving a crisp cause-and-effect proverb.
The result is a saying that feels scriptural and carries the authority of the Bible, while being shorter and blunter than anything actually printed in it.
context.pull: The Bible supplies the idea; the pithy one-liner is the work of centuries of retelling.
